questions.prompt: A woman went to bed well at 10 PM and woke at 6 AM unable to move her right arm or speak. For treatment decisions, when did her stroke 'start'?

choices.a: It can't be estimated, so she's never eligible for treatment
choices.b: 6 AM, when the symptoms were found
choices.c: 10 PM, when she was last known to be well

questions.explanation: Time of onset is taken as the last time the patient was known to be normal. A "wake-up stroke" is timed from when she went to bed; advanced imaging can still identify some such patients who may benefit from treatment.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the 'last known well' rule to timing a stroke.

questions.prompt: A 70-year-old suddenly can't speak and has weakness of the right face and arm, with the leg only mildly affected. Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.explanation: Face and arm weakness greater than leg points to the middle cerebral artery territory; right-sided signs point to the left hemisphere, which is dominant for language in most people, explaining the aphasia.
questions.learning_objective: Localize a middle cerebral artery stroke.

questions.prompt: A patient has a weak, numb left leg with the arm and face nearly normal. Which artery's territory is affected?
questions.explanation: The leg area of the motor and sensory cortex lies on the medial surface of the hemisphere, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery. Left-sided signs mean the right hemisphere.
questions.learning_objective: Localize an anterior cerebral artery stroke.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the emergency non-contrast head CT in suspected acute stroke?

choices.a: To rule out intracranial hemorrhage before thrombolysis
choices.c: To show the ischemic infarct in its first hour

questions.explanation: Early ischemia is often invisible on CT in the first hours, but blood shows immediately. Excluding hemorrhage is essential before giving a thrombolytic.
questions.learning_objective: State the purpose of the initial non-contrast CT in stroke.

questions.prompt: A man with sudden left-sided weakness was last known well 2 hours ago. His glucose is normal and his CT shows no bleeding. Which treatment should be considered now, if he has no contraindications?

choices.c: Wait 24 hours and repeat the CT
choices.d: Give nothing: thrombolysis only works in the first hour

questions.explanation: Within 4.5 hours of last known well, eligible patients with ischemic stroke and no hemorrhage should be considered for IV thrombolysis; those with a large-vessel occlusion are also evaluated for thrombectomy. Anticoagulation isn't an acute stroke treatment.

questions.prompt: Within how long of the patient's last known well time can intravenous thrombolysis generally be given for ischemic stroke?
questions.explanation: IV thrombolysis is given within 4.5 hours of last known well in eligible patients. Mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion extends to 24 hours in selected patients.
questions.learning_objective: Recall the time window for IV thrombolysis.

questions.prompt: After recovering from an ischemic stroke, a 76-year-old is found to have atrial fibrillation. What is the best long-term prevention?

choices.d: Nothing more than blood pressure control

questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation causes cardioembolic strokes; anticoagulation (a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin) substantially reduces recurrence, much more than aspirin. Rate control does not prevent emboli.
questions.learning_objective: Choose secondary prevention for stroke with atrial fibrillation.
